A specimen of everyday typography

Most of what people read on the web is plain text, so the quality of a page comes down to how headings, paragraphs and lists sit together. This page collects each of those pieces in one place. It is meant for looking at spacing and rhythm, not for reading to the end.

Headings in sequence

Third-level heading with a longer title that may wrap on a narrow phone screen

A paragraph after a heading shows the space between them. Good spacing makes the heading feel attached to the text it introduces, not to the paragraph above.

Fourth-level heading

Smaller headings still need to stand apart from body text, even when they are only a little larger.

Inline elements

This sentence has strong text, emphasis, a highlight, a deletion and an insertion. Chemical formulas such as H2O and powers such as 106 need to sit on the line without pushing the lines apart. The HTML specification, written by the WHATWG community, describes semantic markup as markup that says what content is. Small print, such as a licence note, sits quietly at the end. Press Ctrl + S to save, and expect the terminal to print Saved 3 files in reply. Use border-radius for rounded corners, and cite The Elements of Typographic Style when in doubt. He said keep the measure under seventy characters and left it there. The file is draft-1.md now final.md, dated 14 March 2026.

Measure
The width of a block of text, usually counted in characters per line.
Leading
The space between lines of text, named after the lead strips once used in printing.
Widow
A short last line at the top of a column or page.

Typography exists to honor content.

Robert Bringhurst, The Elements of Typographic Style

Code

A short function in a block:

function measure(text) {
  const words = text.trim().split(/\s+/);
  return Math.round(text.length / words.length);
}

The paragraph after a rule and a code block should return to the usual rhythm, with nothing cramped.
